Thanks for the initial materials — the RFP team is working through the security and operations sections. We have a couple of follow-ups specific to continuity acceptance criteria and the actual cutover runbook for multi-region failover that we'd like Redwood to confirm in writing for our procurement & risk committee:  

- Explicit RTO and RPO targets per service tier (hosted API vs dedicated).
- Exact steps and estimated total time for a full active->standby cutover for a single region failure (including DNS, traffic routing, KV cache warming).
- The decision matrix used for triggering cutover vs partial degraded mode (we need the acceptance criteria Crestwood auditors will verify during pre-production testing).
- How model state is preserved during switchover (KV cache, streaming sessions, in-flight requests).
- Evidence of at least one production-scale rehearse or DR test in the last 12 months, with outcomes.

We prefer bullet-point answers we can paste into the RFP appendix. Can you send concise acceptance criteria and point us to the runbook you expect to use during a test? Also include attachments (runbook/PDFs) and any sample test results you can share (redacted).

Laura — thanks for the clarity. Below are compact, acceptance-ready statements your auditors can use; I've also attached our formal acceptance criteria PDF and the operational cutover playbook. Where helpful, I added short notes and references to the runbook sections.

1) RTO / RPO by offering (acceptance statements)
- Hosted API (default): RTO = 5 minutes for control-plane recovery, 99th-percentile API latency target restored within 15 minutes after cutover; RPO = 0 seconds for logged customer requests (all accepted requests are durably stored prior to acknowledgement). (See runbook §2.1–2.3, attachment: redwood_bcp_acceptance_criteria_v1.pdf)
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): RTO = 15 minutes for capacity reallocation and routing changes under committed SLA; RPO = configurable, typical deployment set to 5 minutes for non-critical telemetry and 0 seconds for customer data path. (See runbook §3.4)

2) Full active→standby cutover sequence (high-level, expected total window)
- Detection & decision (0–2 min): Smart routing alerts and SLO breach conditions evaluated by automated policy + on-call approval if required.
- Quiesce new sessions (0–1 min): Ingress layer briefly rejects new long-lived sessions (short window) and returns 503s with retry guidance.
- Prefix/KV flush & durable persistence (up to 2 min): Active nodes commit KV checkpoints to durable store; small window for in-flight streaming segments (see rollback criteria).
- Route update & DNS: Traffic switched to standby pool via global load balancer with TTL-based health checks (DNS + Anycast update) — expected propagation 1–5 min depending on downstream resolvers.
- Warmup & cache priming (5–10 min): Standby region warms model cache using incremental KV snapshots; continuous batching parameters auto-adjust.
- Validation gates (2–5 min): Synthetic probes and canary calls validate latency and output quality; if gates pass, full traffic cutover completes.
- Total observed window: commonly 8–20 minutes end-to-end; worst-case documented plan up to 30 minutes for large-stateful deployments. (See cutover playbook v2 §4.2)

3) Cutover decision matrix / acceptance criteria (auditor-ready)
- Trigger conditions for full cutover: region-wide outage (loss of >= 80% of serving capacity for >2 min), persistent SLO degradation (error% above threshold for >5 min), or manual executive trigger.
- Partial degraded mode: If datastore replication still healthy and latency increases <2x, we maintain degraded/ throttled mode with traffic shaping; acceptance criteria for this mode: synthetic SLA tests remain within degraded band for 15 minutes.
- Reversal criteria: If validation gates fail post-cutover (sustained errors or model quality regression), automatic rollback to previous routing is executed; rollback requires post-mortem before subsequent cutover attempts.

4) Preserving model state & in-flight requests
- KV cache: Checkpointed to shared durable store every 30–90 seconds (configurable). During cutover we replay last checkpoint onto standby; known small window may lose microseconds of uncommitted KV updates — covered in RPO statements above.
- Streaming sessions: We attempt to drain and checkpoint session tokens; long-lived client streams may be asked to reconnect. Streaming SDKs receive retry guidance and idempotency tokens.
- No customer payload is retained by third parties during switchover; all persistence under customer tenancy for Dedicated and under Redwood-managed durable store for Hosted.

5) Evidence of tests (summary)
- We conducted a full-scale rehearse on 2026-06-17 for a hosted workload simulating 4000 rps across 4 regions; artifacts included canary outputs and timing metrics — attached: crestwood_failover_test_results_202608.pdf (redacted).
- We run quarterly table-top exercises and semi-annual live rehearsals with a rolling subset of customers (opt-in).

Attachments included: redwood_bcp_acceptance_criteria_v1.pdf, redwood_cutover_playbook_v2.docx, crestwood_failover_test_results_202608.pdf

If you want a two-page appendix formatted for your RFP, I can provide a plain-text paste-in version. Also looping in Rishi (reliability) and Vivek (security/compliance) for any technical follow-ups.

Laura — quick technical clarifications to support your auditors:  

- Checkpoint cadence: Default KV checkpoint period is 60s; we can tighten to 30s for Dedicated customers as part of onboarding (affects throughput/cost tradeoff).
- DNS TTL: We publish recommended 30s TTL for faster cutover; many customers choose 60–120s based on their supplier constraints.
- Warm-start strategy: Standby applies a prioritized warm list (hot prefixes first) to reduce cold-start latency. This means critical prompt templates and embeddings are available within 90–120s, while full model warm requires longer depending on model size.
- Data residency during cutover: For Private deployments we move traffic within the same tenancy/VPC only; for Hosted we route to nearest compatible region per your policy.

We can provide a short redlined appendix with exact parameter names your engineering team can validate during a dry run.

-Rishi
Rishi Malhotra
